title: PPFD Mapping, Grid Design & Measurement Geometry

content.overview: Canopy-light verification begins with repeatable measurement geometry. A specialist defines the crop plane, sensor orientation, grid spacing, operating state and meter identity before interpreting intensity or uniformity.

vocabulary.definition: Photosynthetic photon flux density reaching a surface, commonly expressed in micromoles per square meter per second.
A repeatable set of spatial positions used to characterize light distribution across a defined canopy area.
The defined height and orientation at which measurements are intended to represent the canopy receiving light.

sections.title: One reading is not a map
sections.body: Fixture spacing, height, reflectance, canopy shape and obstructions create gradients. Use multiple repeatable points rather than relying on the brightest center location.

sections.title: Control geometry between maps
sections.body: Changing sensor height, tilt or grid positions can make before/after comparisons misleading. Record the plane, orientation and fixture operating state.

sections.title: Verify the meter before redesigning the room
sections.body: Instrument type, calibration/verification status and cosine response matter. A suspect meter should not drive major fixture or setpoint changes until checked.

workedExamples: A nine-point grid with one very bright center and dim edges can have an acceptable-looking average while still showing poor distribution.
commonMistakes: Comparing readings from different instruments without verifying method or calibration.
content.practicalApplication: Create a repeatable canopy grid and record PPFD, sensor position, orientation, fixture state and meter identity for each point.
content.summary: Lighting decisions begin with repeatable spatial measurement, not fixture labels or a single peak number.
